lede: Read all eight. Here’s what is actually in the pile. The eight sources contain seven separate lines of argument because Travis Holland’s article appears twice: SRC_7 and SRC_8 are the same Conversation piece republished by ScreenHub. Both repeat the same claims: Jurassic Park used about 50 digital-only creature shots, combined them with large-scale mechanical effects, changed filmmaking, and helped produce a lasting public revival of dinosaur interest. They count as one source, not two confirmations. The rest comprises two video essays, an article explaining Tom van der Linden’s five-part argument, a VFX reaction focused on The Lost World, a cinematography discussion, and a craft analysis of Jurassic Park. The material is strongest on concrete choices—lenses, lighting, practical effects, shot design and post-production—and weakest when a widespread impression becomes an industry-wide verdict. The strongest critics target filmmakers’ use of digital tools, not digital cameras, CGI or visual effects themselves. They blame the freedom those tools provide.

paragraphs.label: The digital image
paragraphs.text: The first video essay points to high dynamic range. Early digital cameras clipped highlights and produced noisy shadows, so the industry pursued more latitude until modern cameras could preserve almost everything. In this critic’s account, the result is a gray, low-contrast image in which nothing is allowed to become properly black or white. The second essay identifies a related shift in lens and focus. Larger digital sensors combined with wider lenses put the camera inside the scene rather than at a distance, while the DSLR-era fascination with shallow depth of field turned backgrounds, extras and locations into blur. Older cinema often stopped down to T5.6, T8 or T11 because the set and world behind the actors mattered. Modern films, by contrast, can look like a YouTube vlog: one face is sharp while the environment is mush. The claim is not that every contemporary film looks ugly, but that a flat, polished, over-controlled default has become unusually common.

paragraphs.label: Choices, not equipment
paragraphs.text: That technical shift has become visual and physical. The second essay says soft light has replaced harder, more directional lighting that gave faces and spaces shape, texture and contrast. Cleaner high-ISO performance creates another temptation: if the camera can see in near-darkness, crews may stop lighting night scenes instead of designing a bright, blue, legible cinematic night, as in The Lord of the Rings. The first essay makes the same point through production design. Superbad was shot digitally on a Panavision Genesis with less dynamic range than an iPhone, yet its red car, mahogany interiors, brown carpets and strong contrast make it look deliberate rather than dull. The equipment did not create that look; choices did. The essay’s comparison is Nancy Meyers’s 1998 The Parent Trap, shot by Dean Cundey, whose rich shadows, bold colors and painterly exteriors contrast with the forgettable modern comedy it resembles. The essay also argues that a six-episode series with 2,000 or 3,000 VFX shots makes decisive lighting difficult: a window or even a room may disappear in post, encouraging crews to shoot blandly, light flatly and avoid commitment.

paragraphs.label: The counterexamples
paragraphs.text: Even defenders of older film concede that modern style is not automatically bad. Dune, The Substance, Smile, Nosferatu and The Brutalist are offered as counterexamples, and the first essay calls Wicked’s much-criticised look a deliberate choice by talented people rather than a mistake. It also cites Zodiac as one of the best uses of digital cinematography and says James Mangold’s The Wolverine and Drive, shot with ARRI’s first digital cinema camera, looked excellent. The broader criticism is that cameras have become better, cheaper and more accessible while filmmakers have become less willing—or less able—to make intentional decisions. The first essay says taste and talent may be declining, though it also acknowledges filmmaking’s volatile combination of taste, talent, money, sacrifice and luck. The second essay’s point is less absolute: modern technology can support deeper focus, stronger contrast, harder light and texture if filmmakers stop treating its flexibility as a crutch. Good writing, storytelling, acting, editing, set dressing, wardrobe, hair and makeup still matter.

paragraphs.label: Van der Linden’s argument
paragraphs.text: Tom van der Linden’s argument, as presented in the article, gives the shift a philosophical backbone. His five reasons concern perceptual realism, the “cinematic look,” indexicality, haptic visuality and cinematic qualia. Modern images can feel less like records of physical worlds than assembled surfaces. Older deep-focus compositions let viewers scan the frame and construct a sense of space, which philosopher Noël Carroll describes as more analogous to ordinary perception. Modern shallow focus narrows that freedom. Digital post-production narrows it further because filmmakers can change backgrounds, performances, lighting, camera positions and even camera movements after the shoot. Indexicality names another difference: with celluloid, light physically struck film to create the image; digital sensors convert light into data, making the result a manipulation of reality rather than a physically formed record. The article also associates film with motion blur from its physical shutter, grain and warmth, versus digital sharpness and pixelated noise.

paragraphs.label: Touch and presence
paragraphs.text: Van der Linden does not treat immersion as optical alone. Laura Marks’s “haptic visuality” describes films experienced through the body as well as the eyes and ears; grain, deep focus, texture, sound, makeup, wardrobe and set dressing can create a richer sensory environment. Van der Linden uses “cinematic qualia”—what a scene feels like to inhabit—to compare the gritty, sweaty physical struggle of Sorcerer with the flat lighting and vanity makeup of Jurassic World Rebirth. Both depict a humid environment, but only one makes its actors appear to suffer inside it. The long-take and constant floating-camera fashion intensify the same problem. Digital technology lets crews roll for hours and move lightweight cameras through a full 360 degrees, but the result can feel like a video-game camera rather than a physical presence in a place. Film reels imposed a finite running time and encouraged precise coverage and editing; endless digital recording can let the take dictate the story. The sources’ larger claim is cumulative: immersion emerges from sequences and sensory feedback loops, not one technical feature.

paragraphs.label: Why Jurassic Park holds up
paragraphs.text: Jurassic Park’s effects remain persuasive because they serve a thriller rather than turning the thriller into a technology demonstration. Spielberg initially planned practical effects—stop-motion raptors and an animatronic T. rex—and added fully digital dinosaurs only after seeing Industrial Light & Magic’s test footage. The finished film contains about 50 digital-only creature shots, but its central illusion comes from a “canny mix” of mechanical effects and carefully limited CGI. Because CGI was an unknown and potentially ruinous quantity, it was used for creatures that could not be made on set, letting artists lavish more attention on each digital frame. The first dinosaur is physically present through animatronics, and practical effects carry the moment when the T. rex’s tongue needs to feel visceral. The craft analysis is especially persuasive in arguing that the film hides weaknesses in rain, darkness, distance, sunset, speed and motion blur. The T. rex chase happens in rain, the dinosaur fight in a dim headquarters, the brachiosaurs at sunset, and the daylight gallimimus stampede uses speed and blur. On DVD-quality viewing, the writer identifies only one visibly bad CGI shot and blames its lighting more than its model or animation.

paragraphs.label: Story before spectacle
paragraphs.text: The effects do not interrupt the story to demand admiration. Jurassic Park is about dinosaurs running amok and killing people; the dinosaurs happen to be realized through CGI. That is why the effects remain persuasive while later effects showcases such as DragonHeart, Spider-Man and some Harry Potter films are described as aging more visibly. The VFX analyst examining The Lost World reaches the same conclusion: practical creatures and digital extensions gave CGI something tangible to blend with, while modern films often put actors in green-screen environments or volumes and ask overworked artists to create nearly everything on deadline. Modern CGI is capable of extraordinary detail, but budget pressure and artist overload can reduce the planning needed for convincing interactions with light, objects and environments. The Jurassic Park craft analysis makes a parallel narrative point: effects are strongest when they facilitate suspense, as Gollum and Life of Pi’s Richard Parker do, rather than replacing story with a dazzle-driven showcase.

paragraphs.label: The disagreements
paragraphs.text: The sources disagree on three substantive points: whether craft or industrial pressure shapes the image, whether visual quality has declined, and what role CGI plays. First, the video essayists blame taste, lost lighting instincts, shallow focus, endless post-production and refusal to commit on set. The Stage 32 cinematographers and commenters counter that finance, algorithms and purse-string decision-makers determine much of the look before creatives can exercise taste. They also say colorists and other post-production workers can damage a cinematographer’s image, and that a DP can attend grading sessions more easily on well-funded films than while working constantly on smaller projects. The strongest evidence for this counterargument is that many indie films still look as good as older studio films because their cinematographers have more freedom. The material contains no reconciliation between that economic explanation and the essayists’ argument about declining taste and talent. Second, the sources disagree about whether decline is real at all. One video lists several contemporary films that look excellent, while a Stage 32 commenter thinks movies are better in many respects and objects mainly to excessive shaky camera, poor casting and green-screen artificiality. Third, the critics call CGI a scapegoat: the real problems are overuse, weak integration and effects-driven storytelling. Jurassic Park shows that limited, story-serving CGI can be revolutionary. No serious source says all-digital production is inherently superior, but no modern VFX practitioner in the pile directly defends the current workflow.

paragraphs.label: Jurassic Park’s legacy
paragraphs.text: Jurassic Park’s legacy goes beyond nostalgia, but its success cannot show that older filmmaking was universally better or every modern effect less convincing. The film combined state-of-the-art puppetry with emerging CGI, helped ILM adopt digital composition more fully, and showed directors that realistic animals, fantasy creatures and eventually digital people could perform without restraint. It also made dinosaurs believable living creatures for a mass audience and reflected the “dinosaur renaissance.” Robert Bakker consulted on the film, which presented dinosaurs as active and bird-related rather than merely slow, cold-blooded monsters. Bakker popularised the term in 1975; the renaissance ran roughly from the 1960s into the 1980s. A generation of later palaeontologists came of age under Jurassic Park’s influence, during what Steve Brusatte called a new “golden age of discovery.” The film’s popularity also produced a “Jurassic Park effect” in ancient-DNA research: scientists who rejected its premises still used the book and movie’s popularity to stress the importance of their technical work. The franchise—five sequels plus games, toys, novels and animated series—helped sustain that public interest.

paragraphs.label: What the pile cannot establish
paragraphs.text: What is honestly missing is hard comparative evidence. No cited study measures the prevalence of flat lighting, shallow focus, CGI or post-production changes across periods. No production budgets or VFX schedules demonstrate that deadlines cause the decline. No direct interview with a contemporary cinematographer, colorist or VFX artist explains where the final look is actually decided. The pile offers a strong craft diagnosis and a memorable Jurassic Park case study, but no evidence here shows how representative either is of filmmaking as a whole.
